rgb: This indoor room has a bare concrete floor, plaster-and-brick walls, a raised brick counter on the left with stacked water jugs (roughly 2 to 2.5 metres away in the early frames), a low cinder-block-supported bench along the rear wall (about 3 metres away), and a small plastic stool next to an orange cloth on the lower-left floor (approximately 1.2 to 1.5 metres away). A young child wearing a dark t-shirt and light pink shorts stands beneath the camera wearer’s elevated viewpoint, initially about 2.5 metres ahead between the brick counter and rear bench in frame 1. During the first two frames, the child’s body faces the camera wearer, although the head turns left in frame 1 and tilts downward in frame 2; the brick counter, floor buckets, and bench are within the child’s arm’s reach, while the camera wearer’s hands enter along the bottom holding a small blue object at immediate-reaching distance (about 0.2 to 0.4 metres away). From frames 2 to 5, the camera angles increasingly downward while the child advances toward the wearer, reducing the separation from around 2.2 metres in frame 2 to 1.7 metres in frame 3, 1.2 metres in frame 4, and 0.8 metres in frame 5. The child passes just right of the plastic stool (roughly 0.3 to 0.5 metres from it), steps onto the orange cloth, raises both arms, and looks straight up at the camera wearer. In frames 4 and 5, the rear bench and upper walls rotate beyond the top and left edges, while a metallic counter with faucets appears at the bottom right within reach of both the wearer and child (about 0.5 metres away). The wearer’s foreground left hand partly blocks the floor, and the lower frame edge crops the child’s lower legs.
depth: The depth map depicts an elevated camera wearer looking downward into an indoor room. On the left are a brick counter and water jugs (~1.5–2.5 m away in frames 1–3), with a low bed/platform in the upper background (~3–4 m away), a plastic stool and white bucket on the left side of the floor (~1.5–2 m away and ~0.3 m apart), and a counter edge entering the bottom-right foreground in frames 4–5 (~0.5–0.8 m away). A young child stands on the floor below and ahead of the wearer, beginning ~2.5 m away beside the brick counter in frame 1 and moving closer through frames 2–5 until directly beneath the wearer at ~0.8–1.0 m. The wearer’s left hand appears in the lower foreground during frames 2–5 at ~0.3–0.5 m, within arm’s reach, and a wall/hanging cloth blocks the left foreground at ~0.3 m in frame 2. While approaching and looking upward at the camera wearer, the child passes about ~0.5 m to the plastic stool’s right and, by frame 5, comes within arm’s reach of both the wearer’s outstretched hand and the lower-right counter. Relative to RGB alone, the depth map distinctly separates the foreground hand, left-side wall obstruction, and standing child from the lit floor despite intense flashlight glare, while also revealing the continuous ground-plane gradient. Still, it is unreliable in the upper-right areas of frames 4–5, where the dim floor and background items (~2.5–4 m away) become uniformly black, and near the bright overexposed hand and cloth, where nearby depth contours blend together.
segmentation: Across all five frames, the segmentation map separates the approaching child in front of and below the camera wearer, showing movement from ~2.5 m away on the left to ~0.8–1.0 m away at the bottom center. It also masks the wearer’s foreground left hand (~0.3–0.5 m away) in frames 2, 4, and 5. In frame 1, the child is approximately ~0.5 m from the left-side counter and bucket. By frames 4–5, the child’s mask joins the wearer’s lower-left hand and the orange floor cloth as one continuous pink area, showing that they overlap in the 2D projection and lie within arm’s reach (~0.3–0.8 m), while the bottom edge partially crops the child’s lower legs. Although the map makes the child’s silhouette and foreground body parts stand out against a blacked-out background, it conveys much less information about spatial layout than the RGB image because the room’s walls, stool, counter, and bed are omitted completely. Object identities and boundaries in the segmentation are highly unreliable: during frames 1–2, the left wall, hanging cloth, plastic stool, bucket, and floor fabrics are incorrectly classified as several 'person' instances and a 'kite'; the wearer’s hand is missed entirely in frame 3; and in frames 4–5, the child, wearer’s hand, and orange cloth on the floor are combined into a single 'person' mask.
pose: Across all five frames, the pose map follows the child’s yellow 2D skeletal keypoints while the child stands below and ahead of the camera wearer. It also shows a magenta hand skeleton for the wearer’s left hand in the bottom-left foreground (~0.3–0.5 m away) in frame 4. In frame 1, the child is on the left at ~2.5 m and appears in left profile, facing the brick counter and standing within arm’s reach of it. Through frames 2–4, the child turns toward the camera wearer; symmetric facial keypoints for the eyes, nose, and ears angle upward toward the lens, and both arms rise above shoulder level as the child closes the distance from ~2.2 m to ~1.2 m. In frame 5, the child occupies the lower-right foreground at ~0.8–1.0 m, faces and looks upward at the wearer, and has both arms lowered to rest within arm’s reach on the foreground counter edge. The legs below the hips are occluded or extend beyond the lower frame boundary. In comparison with the RGB strip, where severe spotlight glare washes out the child’s torso and the wearer’s fingers in frames 4–5, the skeleton map more clearly defines the child’s shoulder-to-hip alignment, head direction, and transition from raised to lowered arms. However, the pose output remains unreliable because it omits the wearer’s visible hand in frames 2, 3, and 5, loses or incorrectly positions the child’s lower-leg keypoints in frames 1, 2, and 4, and offers no spatial depiction of the surrounding walls or furniture.
